transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

**Report PR-AUC as your headline number. Add ROC-AUC only as a secondary figure.**

**Why PR-AUC**
- With 3% positives, ROC-AUC can look great while the model is still not very useful. The false-positive rate divides by the huge pool of non-churners. A model can flag many customers who won't churn and still keep a low false-positive rate. ROC-AUC barely notices those extra flags. - Precision is the number your retention team feels, because it's the share of flagged customers who really would have left. PR-AUC is built on precision and recall, so it tracks how useful the list is. - It's easy to explain to a manager. **Caveats to mention**
- PR-AUC depends on the churn rate. Don't compare it across segments or periods with different base rates unless you show the baseline next to it. ROC-AUC doesn't have this problem, which is why it's still worth a line. - Neither number is a decision. If the team can only contact a fixed number of customers, also report precision and recall at that cutoff. Managers usually find this the most convincing. - Compute everything on held-out data, ideally later in time than the training data. Otherwise any of these metrics will look better than reality. It shows how well we find real churners without flooding the retention team with false alarms."

transcript.text: how can I analyze my customer [shares customers.csv]

Happy to help. I had a look at your table: 1,200 customers, with their plan, segment, city, tenure, monthly spend, recent support tickets, and a churned_next_month column, so it looks like you can see who left. "Analyze" can mean quite different things here, such as understanding who your customers are, finding why some leave, or predicting who is about to leave. What are you hoping to be able to do or decide once you've analyzed them?
I guess I want to see the groups of customers we have. Then I can treat each group differently. Not sure what else to say about it.

That's clear: you want to see your customer groups so you can treat each one differently. I'm assuming you and your team will act on this yourselves, so tell me if that's wrong. Your table already has a `segment` column, so I need to know which groups you mean. Are they the segments you already use, which I'd describe and compare, or do you want me to look for new groups based on how customers behave, such as how long they've stayed, what they spend and how often they contact support?
Not really sure, to be honest. I think the segment column is what we use now, but I don't know if it's the right split. Whatever shows the groups best is fine with me.

Since you're open to whatever shows the groups best, here are two ways to go. I'm assuming you and your team will use the result to decide how to treat each group. I'm also assuming your `segment` column is the split you use today. Tell me if either is wrong. The first option checks whether your current segments are useful. The second looks for groups in the data and compares them to your segments. If you want to know whether your split is the right one, the second option answers that more directly. The first is the faster way to see where you stand.

choices.title: Describe the segments you already have
choices.what: I compare your current segment groups side by side: how many customers each holds, and their typical tenure, monthly spend, support tickets and how many left next month.

choices.title: Find new groups from how customers behave
choices.what: I look for natural groups in your customers based on tenure, monthly spend and support tickets. I leave out churned_next_month when forming the groups, so the groups come from behavior alone. Afterwards I describe each group, including how many left, and compare them to your segment column.

transcript.text: Yeah, the second one sounds good. The segment column is what we use now, and my team will do the acting. I'm not sure what groups will come out of it though.
transcript.pick: Find new groups from how customers behave

transcript.text: I've started a project to find new customer groups from how your customers behave. It won't use your `segment` column or `churned_next_month` to build them. - **What you get back:** a short description of each group, such as who is in it and how it differs from the others. I'll also show how the new groups line up with your current `segment` split. That comparison should tell you whether your split is the right one. - **Churn:** I'll show how many customers in each group left. That should help you decide which group needs which treatment. I'm assuming you and your team will use these groups yourselves, and that grouping on those three behaviors is what you want. Is there anything else about your customers that matters for how you'd treat them, such as the city or the plan, that I should look at when I describe the groups?
Not really sure. Maybe the plan? I don't know if the city matters for how we'd treat them. My team would know better than me what matters for that.

That's fine. I'll describe each new group by its plan as well as by your current segment and churn. I'll leave city out for now, and it's easy to add once your team has said whether it matters. One last thing that affects how I present the groups: once you've seen them, will you decide how to treat each group yourself, or take them to your team to decide?
I'll decide how to treat each group myself, then my team will carry it out.

Thanks, that settles who it's for. You'll decide the treatment and your team will carry it out, so I'll write each group's description in plain terms that you can act on. One practical thing would help me. Roughly how many different treatments could your team handle at once? Two or three, or more? That tells me how many groups to aim for, so you don't end up with more than you can use.
Not sure, to be honest. Maybe two or three? My team would know better what they can handle. Whatever you think makes sense.

Two or three is a sensible range, so I'll aim for three groups. If the data clearly supports only two, I'll show two and tell you why. I'll keep your plan, your current segment and churn alongside each group so you can see how they differ. Your team can then say if three is too many, and I can merge groups. Does that work for you, or is there something you'd want to change before I show you the groups?
Yeah, that works. Go ahead and show me the groups.

Thanks, I've started building your groups. I have no results yet, so I'm not going to guess at what they'll look like. It aims for three groups, or two if the data doesn't clearly support three. - **What you'll see for each group:** who is in it and how it differs from the others. You'll also see its mix of plans, how it lines up with your current `segment` split, and how many of its customers left. - **What I'll do with the results:** I'll point out where the new groups agree or disagree with your current segments. That should show whether your split is worth keeping. City is left out for now. Your team can tell you later if it matters, and I can add it then. If three groups is too many for them, I can merge two.
